extraction.name: Mathematics Aptitude Test of Heuristics (MATH)
extraction.description: A dataset of 12,500 competition mathematics problems, split into 7,500 training and 5,000 test problems. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer. Problems span seven subjects and are tagged with difficulty levels from 1 to 5. The paper also introduces Auxiliary Mathematics Problems and Solutions (AMPS), a mathematics pretraining corpus containing over 100,000 Khan Academy problems and approximately 5 million Mathematica-generated problems.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Bums, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Bums, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, and Jacob Steinhardt. Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021), Track on Datasets and Benchmarks. arXiv:2103.03874v2, 8 November 2021.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: MATH collects problems from mathematics competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Many problems can be collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. The paper describes MATH as carefully curated by the competition mathematics community. The auxiliary AMPS corpus combines problems pulled from Khan Academy with approximately 5 million problems generated using 100 manually designed Mathematica scripts, with around 50,000 exercises generated per script.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: MATH uses mathematics competition problems created by the Mathematical Association of America, including AMC and AIME problems available through the Art of Problem Solving competition community. AMPS uses Khan Academy exercises covering 693 exercise types, reproducible using github.com/Khan/khan-exercises/, and problems generated by the authors' Mathematica scripts.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: MATH final answers are standardized for exact-match assessment: probabilities use simplified fractions; matrix-entry fractions use x/y and other fractions use the LaTeX fraction command; coefficients omit multiplication symbols; variables are alphabetically ordered; and polynomials are ordered by decreasing degree. Equivalent fraction and parenthesis encodings, optional units, spaces, equivalent numerical representations, and different orderings of factors in factorized polynomials are accounted for. During experimental AMPS pretraining, Khan Academy data are upsampled by a factor of 5 and Mathematica data are downsampled by a factor of 2.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: MATH problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX. Mathematical figures are encoded using the Asymptote vector graphics language rather than raster images so text-based models can process them. Final answers are delimited using the LaTeX boxed command. AMPS problems and solutions are also typeset in LaTeX.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each MATH problem has a step-by-step solution and final boxed answer, and is categorized into Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, or Precalculus. Difficulty levels follow AoPS, ranging from 1 for a subject's easiest problems for humans to 5 for its hardest. All 693 Khan Academy exercise modules in AMPS have full step-by-step solutions; 37 of the 100 Mathematica scripts generate full step-by-step LaTeX solutions in addition to final answers.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Mathematica: used in the auxiliary AMPS corpus to generate mathematics problems and final answers; 37 of 100 scripts also generate full step-by-step LaTeX solutions.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that even 40% model accuracy on MATH would have ramifications for cheating on homework. The authors explicitly do not intend the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. They intend its use to better forecast reasoning capabilities and describe solving MATH with machine learning as having profound practical and intellectual significance because of mathematics' broad applicability.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: MATH consists of competition-level problems that are challenging even for humans and require a strong mathematical background and substantial time to solve. Its competitions assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States. The paper states that its answer-equivalence formatting rules cover nearly all practical ways generated and actual solutions can be equivalent. Training models to help students cheat on mathematics exams is explicitly not an intended use.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: MATH is intended for benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability and better forecasting reasoning capabilities. Its 7,500 training problems support model fine-tuning, including training on final answers and step-by-step solutions; its 5,000 test problems support evaluation by normalized exact-match accuracy, with analysis across subjects and difficulty levels. Step-by-step solutions can teach models to generate answer derivations and explanations. AMPS is intended for pretraining models on mathematical fundamentals. The authors do not intend these datasets to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
